task: Our support inbox gets 200 emails a day. How should we triage them?
rewrite:
ambition: A top support-ops lead would not start from a generic urgent/normal/low scheme. They would derive the categories from the inbox itself by coding the contact reason on a few hundred real emails, then ranking by volume and by cost-to-resolve (Pareto). They would also set a response target per category and mark which categories need a human at all and which a macro or help-center article could answer.

agency: The raw material is an export of the last 60-90 days of email threads, with timestamps, who replied, time to first reply, time to resolution, and reopen flags. It is not the helpdesk's summary dashboard or anyone's impression of what the common issues are. It lives in the helpdesk (Zendesk, Help Scout, Front, Gmail) as a CSV/API export. If it is not in reach, I assume a typical B2B/SaaS mix and label every number as an assumption.

acceleration: Contact-reason coding with affinity grouping to build the taxonomy. An urgency x impact matrix (outage or billing or security above how-to questions) to set priority. Native rules for routing and tags (Zendesk triggers, Help Scout workflows, Front rules). An LLM classifier with a handful of labeled examples per category, used only to pre-tag and suggest a priority, with a human confirming on anything low-confidence. Saved replies for the top three to five repeat categories.

accuracy: Hand-label a held-out set of about 100 emails and have a second reviewer label a subset, then check agreement (Cohen's kappa) to show the categories are clear enough. Run the rules or classifier against that set and report precision on the high-priority classes, where a miss costs the most. After rollout, compare median first-response time, reopen rate, and the share of urgent emails answered inside target, before and after, over two weeks. If no export exists, the closest proxy is a manual read of 50 recent emails, which I would flag as weak evidence.

answers.plain:
200 emails a day is roughly 25 an hour over a work day. That's manageable with a light system, but not with an ad hoc one. Here's what I'd do.

**1. Classify every email on two axes**
- **Type:** bug or outage, billing or account, how-to question, feature request, sales or partnership, spam or noise.
- **Urgency:** P1 (service down, security issue, data loss, or a payment problem blocking the customer), P2 (the customer can't do something they need, but there's a workaround), P3 (general questions and requests).

**2. Automate the first pass**
- Filter spam and auto-replies (out-of-office, bounces, newsletters) out of the queue.
- Send an auto-acknowledgment with an expected response time. This cuts duplicate follow-ups.
- Use keyword rules or an LLM classifier to tag type and urgency, and to route. Examples are "refund" or "charge" to billing, and "down" or "can't log in" to the P1 candidate list. Have a human review the tags at first, then spot-check once accuracy is good.
- Link known issues to a macro or a canned reply.

**3. Route by queue, not by person**
- Separate queues for billing, technical, and general, with owners on rotation.
- One person each shift acts as the triager. They review the P1 candidates, fix misroutes, and merge duplicates. That is better than everyone skimming the same inbox.

**4. Set response targets (SLAs)**
- P1: 1 hour. P2: 4–8 business hours. P3: 1 business day.
- Track first-response time and time-to-resolution separately.

**5. Reduce volume at the source**
- Tag every email by topic. The top 5 topics usually account for 50% or more of the volume.
- Fix those with help-center articles, in-product messages, or bug fixes.
- Aim to deflect 20–30% of volume over a few months.

**6. Escalate cleanly**
- Bugs go to engineering as tickets that link back to the email thread, not as forwards.
- Define who gets paged for P1 and what counts as a P1.
- VIP or high-value accounts get flagged automatically.

**7. Review weekly**
- Look at volume by category, SLA misses, reopen rate, and misclassifications. Adjust the rules from what you find.

**Tooling:** Move to a real help desk (Help Scout, Zendesk, Front, or Plain) if you're still in a shared Gmail inbox. They provide tagging, assignment, macros, SLAs, and reporting. For a team of 2–4, Help Scout or Front is usually enough.

**To start:** spend a week tagging by hand to see the real category mix. Then build the rules and SLAs from that data.

If you tell me your team size, current tooling, and product type, I can make this more specific. I can also draft the classification rules or a classifier prompt.
answers.nudge:
# Triaging 200 support emails a day

I don't know your product, team size, or tooling, so this is a default design to adapt. At 200 a day (about 25 an hour), you're past the point where an inbox can work as a queue. You need a system with routing, priorities, and feedback loops.

## 1. Set the goals first

Triage exists to hit explicit targets, so decide these before you build anything:

- **First-response SLA by tier.** For example: P1 within 1 hour, P2 within 4 business hours, P3 within 1 business day.
- **Resolution targets**, tracked separately from response time.
- **Quality bar.** Use CSAT, reopen rate, and a weekly sample of 10–20 tickets scored against a rubric.

## 2. Move off a shared inbox

If the emails still land in Gmail or Outlook, move to a ticketing tool (Zendesk, Help Scout, Front, Intercom, or Plain). You need ownership, status, tags, SLA timers, macros, and reporting. Shared inboxes cause duplicate replies and dropped threads, and they give you no data.

## 3. Classify each email on three axes

Don't use a single "priority" field. Tag each ticket with:

| Axis | Values | Drives |
|---|---|---|
| **Type** | Bug/outage, billing/refund, account/access, how-to, feature request, sales/partnership, abuse/security, spam | Who handles it |
| **Urgency** | P1 service down, data loss, security, or payment failure. P2 blocked, with no workaround. P3 degraded, with a workaround. P4 question or feedback. | Order and SLA |
| **Customer value** | Plan tier, ARR, renewal date, churn-risk flags | Tiebreaker and escalation |

Urgency comes from impact and blockage, not from the sender's tone or ALL CAPS. Customer value breaks ties within a tier. It shouldn't override a real P1 from a small customer.

## 4. Automate the first pass

At 200 a day, roughly 60–70% of volume is usually repeatable. Layer the automation:

1. **Spam and noise filter.** Auto-close out-of-office replies, bounces, newsletters, and no-reply notifications.
2. **Rules.** Match keywords, sender domain, and form fields. Examples: "refund" or "charge" routes to billing, and a VIP domain gets priority.
3. **LLM classifier.** Have a model tag type, urgency, language, sentiment, and a one-line summary. Then:
   - Start in **shadow mode**. It tags but doesn't route. Compare its tags against humans on about 300 tickets.
   - Go live only for categories where it's at least 90–95% accurate, and send low-confidence cases to a human.
   - Never let it auto-downgrade anything mentioning security, legal, data loss, or cancellation.
4. **Suggested replies and knowledge-base links.** Give agents a draft to edit. Auto-send only for narrow, low-risk categories such as password reset instructions or order status, and only after a few weeks of measured accuracy.
5. **Deflection upstream.** Mine the top 10 ticket types and fix them with help-center articles, in-app messages, or a contact form that asks for the right fields (account ID, steps, screenshot). Fewer vague emails means less triage work.

## 5. Routing and staffing

- **Tiers.** Tier 1 handles how-to, account, and billing basics with macros. Tier 2 handles bugs and complex cases. Engineering gets escalations only through a defined handoff.
- **Capacity.** At about 7 minutes average handle time, 200 tickets is about 23 agent-hours a day. Plan on **4 agents** once you allow for breaks, meetings, and harder tickets, plus coverage for spikes.
- **Rotating triage owner.** One person per shift (or per day) watches the queue, fixes misroutes, and spots incidents. Without a named owner, triage becomes "someone will get to it."
- **Pull, don't pick.** Agents take the top ticket in their queue, ordered by SLA deadline. Don't let people cherry-pick easy ones.

## 6. Escalation and incident handling

- **Engineering escalation.** Use a template: repro steps, account ID, logs, impact, and customer tier. File it in the bug tracker and link it to the ticket, so engineering gets no raw forwards.
- **Incident detection.** Alert when 5 or more tickets share a tag or keyword within 30 minutes. Then post one status update and use a macro for replies, rather than answering 40 people individually.
- **Security and legal.** Give these an automatic fast lane to a named owner, outside the normal queue.
- **Angry or churn-risk customers.** Give them a human reply within the hour, ideally from a senior agent.

## 7. Measure it

Review weekly:

- First-response time and resolution time by tier, plus SLA breach rate.
- Backlog age (the oldest ticket matters more than the average).
- Reopen rate and CSAT, and the classifier's accuracy against human corrections.
- Tickets per category, with trends. Each one is a product, docs, or UX issue.
- Cost per ticket and automation rate.

Send a monthly "top 5 ticket drivers" report to product and engineering. This is the most valuable output of support, and it lowers volume over time.

## 8. Rollout

1. **Week 1:** Move to a ticketing tool. Define the taxonomy (about 10–15 types), the urgency rubric, and the SLAs.
2. **Weeks 2–3:** Add rules, macros, and spam filtering. Start the rotating triage owner. Begin labeling data.
3. **Weeks 4–6:** Run the LLM classifier and draft replies in shadow mode, then turn on routing for the high-accuracy categories.
4. **Ongoing:** Do a monthly taxonomy cleanup, a weekly quality review, and deflection work on the top ticket drivers.

## Common mistakes

- Making the taxonomy too granular. Over 20 categories means inconsistent tagging.
- Triaging by arrival order or by who emailed most recently.
- Automating replies before measuring accuracy.
- Tracking only response time. Fast, unhelpful replies hurt you.
- Never feeding ticket themes back to product.

To tailor this, I'd need to know your product type (B2B SaaS, e-commerce, or something else), team size, current tooling, and how many tickets are P1/P2 today. With a sample of anonymized emails, I could draft the taxonomy, the urgency rubric, and the classifier prompt.
answers.skill:
I found no export or email threads in the working directory, so I haven't read any real emails. I can't honestly "code a sample of real emails" or report observed volumes. Everything below about the mix is an assumption, marked as such. The plan is built so the first step on real data can confirm or overturn it.

## 1. Assumed mix (replace with real counts)

These are hypotheses for a typical B2B/SaaS or e-commerce inbox. About 200 emails a day is roughly 4,000 over 20 working days.

| Group | Assumed share | Assumed handling cost |
|---|---|---|
| How-to / "where is X" | 25% | Low (2 min) |
| Billing: invoices, receipts, plan changes | 18% | Low–Med (4 min) |
| Order/delivery status or account access (login, password reset) | 15% | Low (3 min) |
| Bug / something broken | 14% | High (15–30 min, often needs escalation) |
| Refund / cancellation / chargeback threat | 8% | Med–High (8 min, has money or churn risk) |
| Outage / security / data issue | 2% | Very high, but rare |
| Feature request / feedback | 6% | Low |
| Sales, partnership, vendor spam | 8% | Near zero |
| Other / unclear | 4% | Med (needs a read to classify) |

The ranking by volume × cost would probably put bugs, billing and refunds at the top of the workload. How-to would be the biggest by count but cheap. That ranking is the first thing to check against real data.

## 2. Taxonomy, priority, targets, owner, deflection

Priority = urgency × impact (P1 = act now, P4 = batch).

| Group | Priority | First-response target | Owner / queue | Saved reply or help article? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Outage / security / data loss | P1 | 30 min, 24/7 on-call | Escalations queue → on-call engineer | No. Use an acknowledgment macro only. |
| Refund / cancel / chargeback / legal | P2 | 2 business hours | Billing-Retention queue | Partly. Macro for policy, human decides. |
| Bug / broken feature | P2 (P1 if it blocks all use) | 4 business hours | Tier 2 / Product-support queue | Partly. Use a "we're investigating" macro and a known-issues article. |
| Billing (invoice, receipt, plan change) | P3 | 1 business day | Billing queue | Yes. Most are receipts or invoice copies. |
| Account access / order status | P3 (P2 if the user is fully locked out) | 4 business hours | Tier 1 | Yes. Self-serve reset and tracking articles. |
| How-to | P4 | 1 business day | Tier 1 | Yes. Help-center article first. |
| Feature request | P4 | 2 business days | Tier 1 → product-feedback tag | Yes. Acknowledgment macro. |
| Sales / vendor / spam | P4 | None | Auto-route to sales alias or close | Yes. Auto-reply or filter. |
| Other / unclear | P3 | 1 business day | Triage queue (rotating human) | No. Reclassify, then route. |

Two modifiers raise priority one level, whatever the group. The first is a high-value account (a VIP/plan-tier field). The second is a second contact on the same issue within 24 hours (a repeat or reopen).

## 3. Implementation as helpdesk rules

Order matters. Rules run top-down and the first match wins, except for the tag and priority rules.

1. **Spam/vendor filter.** If the sender is on a vendor/noreply list, or the subject matches "partnership|SEO|guest post", send it to the sales alias and close it.
2. **P1 keywords.** If the subject or body matches "outage|down for everyone|breach|unauthorized|data (loss|leak)|can't access any", set P1, assign to Escalations, and page on-call.
3. **Money/legal keywords.** If it matches "refund|cancel|chargeback|dispute|lawyer|GDPR delete", set P2 and assign to Billing-Retention.
4. **Form or channel fields.** If the contact form has a "topic" dropdown, map it directly to a queue. This is more reliable than text matching, and I'd add the dropdown if you lack one.
5. **Text rules for billing, access, order and how-to.** Match "invoice|receipt|charge" → Billing. Match "password|login|2FA|locked" → Tier 1 with the access tag. Match "where is my order|tracking" → Tier 1 with the order tag.
6. **VIP bump.** If the account tier is enterprise or top-tier, raise priority one level.
7. **Reopen bump.** If a ticket reopens or a second email arrives within 24 hours, raise priority one level and notify the original owner.
8. **Catch-all.** Anything unmatched goes to the Triage queue with the `needs-review` tag.
9. **SLA timers.** Attach the timers from the table by priority, with an alert at 75% of the target.

**LLM pre-tag (suggestion only).** On ticket creation, an LLM reads the thread and writes three fields: suggested group, suggested priority, and a one-line reason. It has no authority:
- The suggestion appears as a sidebar or internal note, not in the routing fields.
- The agent confirms or changes it with one click. The final label is stored separately from the suggestion, so you can measure disagreement.
- The model never sends replies and never closes tickets. It never downgrades P1 or P2 rules on its own. Keyword rules 2 and 3 still fire regardless.
- Log model name, prompt version and confidence for every suggestion.

## 4. How we'll know it works

**Step 0, before launch: build the truth set on real data.**
- Pull the 90-day export. Randomly sample about 100 emails as a held-out set. Don't use them to write rules or prompts. Stratify lightly so each high-priority group has at least 10 examples, even if that means oversampling.
- Reviewer A labels all 100 against the taxonomy. Reviewer B independently labels a random 30–40 without seeing A's labels.
- Report Cohen's kappa and raw percent agreement on group, and separately on priority. Rough bar: kappa ≥ 0.7 is workable. Below that, the taxonomy definitions are fuzzy and need fixing before any model is measured. Resolve disagreements and write the rule that settles each one.
- Run the LLM pre-tag on the held-out set. Report precision and recall per group, with precision called out for P1 and P2 (outage, refund/legal, bug). With 100 emails, a group with 8 examples has a wide confidence interval, so report the counts next to each percentage. Target precision of ≥ 85% on P1/P2 suggestions. For P1, recall matters more than precision, because a missed outage costs more than a false alarm.

**Before vs. after, two weeks each.**
- Baseline: the 14 days before launch, taken from the export.
- Compare the 14 days after launch on:
  - **Median and 90th-percentile first-response time**, overall and per group.
  - **Reopen rate** (reopened ÷ closed).
  - **On-time urgent replies**: the share of P1/P2 tickets answered inside target.
- Caveats to report with the numbers: two weeks of data is small, so check for seasonality, holidays and volume spikes in either window. Where volumes differ a lot, compare by group rather than overall. A before/after comparison can't prove the cause. If it's easy to do, route one queue or one shift first and use the rest as a comparison.
- Also track agent override rate on LLM suggestions, plus how many tickets land in the catch-all queue. A catch-all share above about 10% means the rules need work.

## What would sharpen this most

A **90-day export with first-reply and resolution times**, with timestamps, reopen flags, tags or subject lines, and the raw message bodies. It would replace every assumed percentage above with measured volume and handling cost. It would also give the baseline for the before/after comparison.

If you drop the file into this directory, I'll run the sampling and coding and rebuild the tables from the real data.
